title: List services that are running now
summary: On most current Linux systems, systemd starts and manages background programs called services, such as networking, printing and SSH. This command lists the services that are active right now.

aliases.text: how to see running daemons linux

prerequisites: A terminal on the Linux computer where systemd is the init system (see the linux-init-system-check card if unsure)

steps.explain: List the systemd services that are running right now. The output opens in a pager: scroll with the arrow keys and press q to return to the prompt. Look at the ACTIVE and SUB columns: 'active' and 'running' mean the service is working now. The bottom of the output shows a count of listed units.
steps.expect: A table with UNIT, LOAD, ACTIVE, SUB and DESCRIPTION columns. Rows like cron.service with loaded active running, then a footer with a unit count.

alternatives.explain: Show all running units, not only services. This also includes timers, sockets, mount points and other unit types.
alternatives.expect: Like the first list, but rows can end in .timer, .socket, .mount, .device and other suffixes besides .service.

steps.explain: If the command prints 'System has not been booted with systemd as init system (PID 1)', this computer does not use systemd, or you are inside a container. Systemd commands cannot list services there. Check the init system with the linux-init-system-check card.

warnings: Inside a Docker container, or on a system without systemd, the command fails with 'System has not been booted with systemd as init system (PID 1)'. The services are not broken; systemd just does not manage this machine.
The list shows services that are running at this moment only. A service that is stopped or failed is not in this list.

source.title: systemctl manual; card written and verified in the lnxhelp sandbox
